$comment: THE PIN. What this gate grades WITH, recorded so a verdict is attributable to a build.
EVERY `downloadUrl` HERE NAMES EXACTLY ONE RELEASE OR ONE REGISTRY VERSION, and that is a rule
rather than a coincidence: the validator's own README publishes a download that resolves to
whatever upstream released most recently, and a source like that cannot agree with a recorded
version for longer than upstream stays still. A source that names no single version is refused
at the acquisition step rather than resolved there.
A VERSION-ADDRESSED SOURCE IS NOT AN IMMUTABLE ONE, so the digest does not get to relax.
Upstream replaces published assets in place, so the sha256 is still the only thing that can
catch the bytes behind a fixed address changing. An EMPTY sha256 is refused, not accepted: an
unrecorded identity read as 'accept anything' is the failure with extra steps. The run prints
the version and the digest it observed, so recording one is a deliberate act with the evidence
in front of you, in a reviewed commit that says which build the verdicts after it came from.
`version` is compared against the version THE PINNED SOURCE NAMES. A GitHub release download is
/releases/download/<tag>/validator_cli.jar, so the tag is the version; the package registry URL
carries its version as its last segment. Neither needs the artifact to be executed to be
identified, which is what keeps the comparison testable with no JVM.
`terminologyServer` is null, and that is a DECLARATION rather than a silence. It is passed to
the validator explicitly (-tx n/a), so the endpoint record in the verdict is the configured set
rather than a guess at a default, no generated content leaves the runner for terminology
resolution, and the verdict does not depend on a live public service that would make it
reproducible by rerun rather than by seed. The consequence is stated in the verdict, in the
coverage declaration and on the published limitations page: terminology-bound checks are not
part of this verdict.
